column1: On x86-64, which two CPU privilege rings do mainstream OS kernels actually use, and what distinguishes them?
column2: Ring 0 (kernel mode, full privileged instruction access) and Ring 3 (user mode, restricted). The hardware raises a General Protection Fault (#GP) if ring-3 code executes privileged instructions like lgdt, wrmsr, or in/out.

column1: What happens atomically when a user process executes the x86-64 SYSCALL instruction?
column2: The CPU saves the return address and stack pointer into MSRs (IA32_LSTAR, IA32_FMASK), switches to ring 0, and jumps to the kernel's syscall entry point — all without an explicit interrupt descriptor lookup.

column1: Why does a Linux syscall round-trip cost ~100–300ns on modern hardware with KPTI enabled?
column2: Because Kernel Page Table Isolation forces TLB flushes and cache pollution on every ring transition as a Spectre/Meltdown mitigation.

column1: What is the policy-mechanism separation principle in OS design, and give a concrete Linux example.
column2: The kernel provides mechanisms (e.g., scheduling queues) while policy (which process runs when) is configurable or user-space driven. Example: SCHED_FIFO (soft-realtime) and SCHED_BATCH (throughput) use the same scheduling mechanism but different policies.

column1: Why must the kernel use copy_from_user/copy_to_user instead of directly dereferencing user pointers?
column2: To prevent TOCTOU (time-of-check-to-time-of-use) races — the user-space mapping could change between the validation check and actual dereference, and the kernel must never trust caller-supplied pointers directly.

column1: What is the only legitimate path for a transition from ring 3 to ring 0 on x86-64?
column2: A system call trap (SYSCALL) or a hardware interrupt — both routed through kernel-controlled, boot-time-configured entry points (IDT/MSRs) that are not writable from user space.

column1: What are the three core invariants an OS must maintain simultaneously according to OS theory first principles?
column2: Safety (no unauthorized memory/instruction/device access), Liveness (guaranteed forward progress, no starvation/deadlock), and Transparency (consistent abstractions regardless of physical resource state).

column1: What role does the U/S bit in a page-table entry play in privilege enforcement?
column2: When set, the page is accessible from ring 3 (user mode); when clear, any ring-3 access to that page triggers a page fault, enforcing kernel/user memory isolation at the hardware level.

column1: What is the purpose of the Virtual File System (VFS) layer in Linux?
column2: It provides a unifying abstraction (open, read, write, close, ioctl) that decouples the file system interface from specific implementations, allowing multiple file systems to coexist and be accessed through a common hierarchical namespace via mount points.

column1: What is the role of the superblock in a file system's architecture?
column2: It stores critical metadata about the file system itself, such as total block count, free block count, and other structural information needed to interpret the rest of the on-disk layout.

column1: How does the Linux kernel split the 64-bit virtual address space between user and kernel?
column2: User space occupies the lower half (0x0000000000000000–0x00007fffffffffff, 128 TiB), while the kernel is mapped into the upper half starting at 0xffff800000000000.

column1: What hardware mechanism translates virtual to physical addresses on every memory access, and what caches its recent results?
column2: The Memory Management Unit (MMU) performs translation via a multi-level page table walk (PGD→P4D→PUD→PMD→PTE on x86-64); the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) caches recent translations to avoid repeated walks.
